## The problem, in one measurement

`gate.greenCheckpoint.candidate` declares `changeInCandidate.judgingSha` as its
change signal. That value follows the gate's in-flight candidate, which is drawn
from the staging tip — **335 commits in 24 hours** on this fleet
(`git rev-list --count --since="24 hours ago" staging`, 2026-07-27).

Every one of those steps moved the cell's digest. So every fact that declared
`dependsOn: ['gate.greenCheckpoint.candidate']` was re-marked STALE, and every
orient that carried such a fact re-rendered a 412-byte paragraph asking the
reader to re-verify — for every agent, on every wake, 335 times a day.

But re-read what the cell is *for*: "WHICH commit the gate is judging — a red
about a candidate that does not contain your change reads as *your fix did not
work* instead of *your fix was not present*." The question is not which sha. It
is **whether the gate is judging your change**, and that answer —
`judgingContainsPath` — moves only when *your* file lands, not when the other
334 commits do.

That is D-018 A.2's rule exactly: *push what changed the SENDER's own model;
everything else stays pull.*

## The declaration

`CellSpec.materiality` is optional. Omitting it means "every change is material",
which is the default and today's behaviour for every other cell.

```ts
materiality: {
  path: 'changeInCandidate.judgingContainsPath',
  why: 'judgingSha follows the staging tip — measured 335 commits/24h — but the question this cell exists to answer is "is the gate judging MY change"…',
}
```

`path` is a **second dot-path into the same resolver result**, extracted from the
**same dispatch** (`readCell` returns it as `material`). It is a lens, not a
computation: no extra resolver call, and nothing the registry has to interpret.

### Why a path and not a threshold DSL

The obvious alternative is a reduction rule — `{ kind: 'threshold', at: 1 }`, so
`consecutiveReds` 0→1 is a flip and 1→2 is a bump. It is refused, on this
registry's own precedent. `cell-registrations.ts` records **twice** that when a
declaration cannot state something honestly, the fix belongs in the **resolver**,
not the declaration. A registry computing `reds >= 1` would be the registry
*deriving a verdict* — exactly what D-038 axis 5 forbids one level up.

So `gate.greenCheckpoint.verdict` genuinely wants materiality and deliberately
does **not** have it: its resolver exposes no coarse verdict field to name. When
it does, the declaration is one line. Until then it stays un-gated rather than
growing a DSL.

### Why `why` is required

Every other field in this registry fails **loudly** when it is wrong. This one
fails **silently, in the confident direction**: a cell naming the wrong material
path stops telling agents about real changes, and nothing surfaces to say so.
A reader told "3 changes were not raised" must be able to check the claim that
they did not matter. Suppression that cannot be audited is not a threshold, it is
a blind spot.

## What the fold does with it

`FactDependencyStatus` gains a fourth value, `immaterial`, and it is deliberately
*not* a fourth kind of unknown — it is a **positive** verdict. The raw value
moved, the declared material answer did not, and we know both. So it does not
block a clean roll-up the way `undeterminable` does.

| verdict | when | in the fold |
|---|---|---|
| `fresh` | raw digest unchanged | the existing line |
| `immaterial` | raw moved, material answer held | one short clause; raw values **dropped** |
| `changed` | material answer moved (**or** no material anchor) | the full loud paragraph |
| `undeterminable` | could not compare | unchanged |

There is **no fourth roll-up status**. `cell-contract.ts` states the rule for its
sibling enum: adding a code is a contract change, because every caller's branch
set changes with it. A materially-unchanged fact is not stale, so it rolls up as
`fresh`, and the news travels in `immaterial[]` plus the note.

### The measurement

Per fact, per orient, for one candidate step:

| | note | deps | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| ungated (today) | 412 | 192 | **719** |
| materiality-gated | 55 | 179 | **349** |

**51% smaller**, and it scales linearly: a fold carrying 12 such facts drops from
8628 to 4188 bytes *per orient, per agent*. Asserted as a test, not a claim —
`dependency-staleness.test.ts` → "P-021 measurement".

Three things produce that saving, and each is principled rather than cosmetic:

1. **`was`/`now` are dropped** from an `immaterial` entry. Those are literally
   "every intermediate version" — the bytes the item says the reader should stop
   receiving.
2. **`materialPath` is not copied** onto each verdict row. It is a per-cell
   registry constant; repeating it per row is denormalisation *and* a
   transcription that rots when the resolver's shape moves.
3. **The note goes quiet.** `note` is the line rendered loudly wherever the fact
   is delivered, and its job is to prompt an action. A version bump asks for
   nothing, so a paragraph explaining it is pure cost.

> ⚠ The first attempt at this **failed its own measurement** — the gated verdict
> came out *larger* than the ungated one (4325 vs 3854 bytes), because the audit
> metadata added per row outweighed the short shas removed. The fix came from
> measuring where the bytes actually were, not from reasoning about it. If you
> extend this, measure first.

## The two failures the design is shaped around

### 1. Materiality may SUPPRESS a raw change; it must never MASK a material one

The material path and the change-signal path are **siblings in one result**, not
a value and a summary of it, so they move independently. The same candidate can
be re-judged (`judgingSha` static) while your file lands (`judgingContainsPath`
flips).

So the material answer is compared **first**, before the raw digest — a material
change is reported `changed` even when the raw value sat still. Gating materiality
behind "did the raw value change?" would report that case `fresh`: a false
all-clear on precisely the change the reader cares most about, produced by the
mechanism meant to protect them.

Every unanchored case degrades to the **loud** reading, never the quiet one:

- a dependency filed before this field existed (no `materialDigest`);
- a declared path that does not resolve now (registration drift);
- a materiality path **re-aimed** since the fact was filed — the stored anchor and
  the fresh reading answer different questions, which is `FactDependency.subject`'s
  rule verbatim: a comparison that silently changes the question does not give a
  weaker answer, it gives a wrong one.

### 2. A subscription never gets materiality—or assessment—applied silently

`state:subscribe` now takes `target: 'assessment' | 'measurement' | 'material'`.
On an assessed cell, an operand-free subscription defaults to `assessment`: wake
when the resolver-owned semantic code changes, even if the raw measurement did not.
`target:'measurement'` explicitly watches the headline/raw value, and
`target:'material'` explicitly watches the declared coarse lens. The retired `of`
argument is refused rather than translated; `of:'value'` maps conceptually to
`target:'measurement'`, never to assessment.

A valued predicate on an assessed cell must name its target. The tool refuses an
ambiguous operand rather than guessing which domain it belongs to. It also refuses
`target:'material'` when the cell declares no materiality path and
`target:'assessment'` when it declares no assessment. Silently re-pointing a
caller's condition at any sibling path does not narrow it—it evaluates it against a
**different domain**. Concretely, `on:{op:'ne',value:'4c871fdc'}` aimed at a boolean
containment or enum assessment path is true on the first poll, so the agent wakes on
a condition never established. A wake is an interrupt (D-044); explicit targets keep
the raw measurement, assessment meaning, and materiality threshold distinct.

## Where this sits relative to D-044

D-044 draws the line: **coupling decides relevance, surprisal decides whether
something is worth an interrupt** — and a pull surface needs no surprisal gate,
because the caller asked.

So materiality gates what arrives **unasked**: the wake, and the staleness verdict
that rides along on every orient. It does **not** delete anything. `state:read`
still returns the current value; `immaterial[]` still names what was suppressed.
The fold carries the rest — silently, which is the item's own word.

## Adding one

1. Confirm the resolver **already exposes** the coarse answer. If it does not,
   fix the resolver — do not compute it here.
2. Check the churn is **real and measured**. The P-020 verdict rule applies: add
   a knob where churn is measured, never everywhere it would fit. Of the five
   registered cells, exactly one has it — `deploy.3070.sha` moves 13×/24h and
   every move is genuinely news; two others are booleans, where a change already
   *is* a verdict flip.
3. Declare `path` + `why`. The registration gate refuses a path equal to
   `changeSignal.path` (a declared no-op), an empty `why`, and materiality on an
   event-signalled cell (there is no resolver result to path into).
